evidence_quotes.text: For years, engineering bandwidth was the expensive thing.
On the Claude Code team, coding is rarely the slow part anymore.
The bottleneck moved from coding to everything around coding: Verification, Review, XFN, Security.

core_insights.generalization: Any pipeline where one stage becomes near-free will shift the system bottleneck downstream; measure the new constraint before optimizing the old one.
core_insights.insight: When code generation becomes fast, the constraint migrates to verification, review, cross-functional alignment, and security — i.e., the harness around the code, not the code production itself. The Claude Code team reports coding 'is rarely the slow part anymore.'
core_insights.why_it_matters: It inverts where investment should go in agentic engineering systems: throughput, latency, and headcount planning should target verification and review capacity (test synthesis, diff triage, review routing, security scanning), not generation speed. Teams that keep optimizing generation will see diminishing returns and growing review queues.

evidence_quotes.text: When teammates disagree on a design, having Claude prototype both approaches and examining the actual artifact is faster and cheaper than lengthy arguments.
Generating multiple PR versions with Claude to compare technical approaches and human impact.

core_insights.generalization: Where the cost of producing a candidate artifact approaches zero, selection should be based on produced artifacts rather than on pre-hoc argument; the comparison criteria become the scarce, valuable asset.
core_insights.insight: Technical disagreements are resolved by generating multiple competing prototypes/PR versions with the model and comparing the artifacts, rather than by argument or deliberation. This is a concrete decision mechanism: candidate generation plus empirical comparison replaces opinion-driven debate.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It is a cheap, repeatable selection procedure that can be applied to architecture choices, API designs, and human-impact tradeoffs. For agent systems it suggests building explicit 'generate N variants, then compare against criteria' loops rather than single-shot generation followed by review meetings.

evidence_quotes.text: Documentation and design docs quickly go out of date, whereas keeping specs and source of truth directly inside the codebase leverages AI updating loops
Claude code commits and repository-embedded specs act as the primary knowledge base for onboarding

core_insights.generalization: For any AI-maintained knowledge store, choose the storage location that a reliable automated write loop already touches; otherwise the store decays.
core_insights.insight: The source of truth is relocated into the codebase: specs, docs, and knowledge live next to the code so that the model's update loop keeps them current, and they serve as the primary onboarding knowledge base. External wikis/design docs are treated as inherently decayed.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is a context-placement decision: colocating durable knowledge with the artifact it governs gives the agent a maintainable retrieval surface and eliminates a synchronization problem between two stores. It implies a design principle — put machine-maintained context where the machine already writes, instead of in a separate doc system that drifts.

evidence_quotes.text: Every engineer uses Claude Code and Co-work daily.
Claudify everything you can.
Provide explicit permission to kill old processes.
People don't delete processes on their own; leaders must name the ones that can go.

core_insights.generalization: To change an engineering system's operating point, pair a hard constraint (mandate) with an explicit depreciation permission; otherwise the system retains its old invariants.
core_insights.insight: Rollout uses 'forcing functions': non-negotiable top-down mandates paired with explicit bottom-up permission to delete processes and adapt local rituals. The key operational lever is that leaders must name which processes can die, because people do not delete processes on their own.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Adoption of transformative tooling fails not from lack of capability but from unpriced legacy process. Naming and authorizing removal of specific processes is the mechanism that converts a new tool into a new default; without it, old rituals persist and consume the freed capacity.

evidence_quotes.text: Onboarding ramp time goes down because engineers ship real code in week one.
PR cycle time shortens and queue depth stops being a leading complaint.
Claude-assisted commits become the default rather than the exception.

core_insights.generalization: Measure whether the new path is the default path (share of work through it), not only whether it is faster when used.
core_insights.insight: Adoption is baselined with three observable signals: onboarding ramp time (new engineers ship real code in week one), PR cycle time (queue depth stops being the leading complaint), and Claude-assisted commit share moving from exception to default.
core_insights.why_it_matters: These are cheap, generalizable instrumentation targets for any AI-assisted engineering rollout. Claude-assisted commit share in particular is an operational telemetry metric that tells you whether assistance is the default path or a side experiment — a distinction that usually predicts whether the workflow change is durable.

evidence_quotes.text: Human judgment on what actually needs code review.

core_insights.generalization: When a downstream human stage becomes the bottleneck, convert it from a uniform gate into a risk-prioritized router.
core_insights.insight: Code review is reframed as selective: humans apply judgment about what actually needs review rather than uniformly gating all changes. This turns review into a routing/classification problem rather than a blanket stage.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If generation volume rises, uniform human review becomes the throughput ceiling. Treating review as risk-based routing (which diffs, which reviewers, which checks) is the concrete way to keep the pipeline from stalling, and it implies an explicit classifier or policy layer between generation and merge.

evidence_quotes.text: Fiona attempted to update CLI tooling with a holiday theme and wanted to make Claude look like a snowman, but a designer reviewed it and pointed out it looked like Mr. Peanut.
Humans are still essential for taste, brand alignment, risk tolerance

core_insights.generalization: Automated verification covers specifiable properties; judgment-dependent properties stay with humans and should be routed explicitly rather than assumed covered.
core_insights.insight: Human review retains responsibility for taste, brand alignment, and risk tolerance even when the model executes competently — a visual/brand failure (a snowman asset that read as Mr. Peanut) was caught by a designer, not by the generating loop.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It locates a residual class of failures that execution-side quality checks do not catch: judgment-dependent, context-dependent, non-verifiable-by-construction properties. For system design, this argues for placing human gates specifically at taste/brand/risk boundaries rather than assuming verification coverage is complete.

Overview

  • Speaker: Fiona Fung
  • Channel: Claude
  • Main topic: Running an AI-native engineering organization and adapting team norms around Claude Code and Co-work
  • Purpose: To share lessons and tactical insights on how engineering organizations must adapt their processes, norms, and team structures when AI makes coding significantly faster and shifts bottlenecks away from writing code. Fiona Fung, manager of the Claude Code and Cowork team at Anthropic, discusses how engineering bottlenecks have shifted from coding and writing bandwidth to verification, review, and cross-functional collaboration. She outlines five major team norms that had to be rewritten—code review, onboarding, planning, hiring, and org shape—arguing that code is now the source of truth, building is cheap while arguing is expensive, and leaders should maintain individual contributor work.

Topic Map

The Shift in Bottlenecks

  • Explanation: Engineering bandwidth used to be the expensive limiting factor, driving heavy planning, scoping, and review processes to protect that resource. With AI coding tools like Claude Code, coding is rarely the slow part anymore, causing bottlenecks to shift from writing code to verification, review, cross-functional alignment, and security.
  • Key claims:
    • For years, engineering bandwidth was the expensive thing.
    • On the Claude Code team, coding is rarely the slow part anymore.
    • The bottleneck moved from coding to everything around coding: Verification, Review, XFN, Security.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing early 2000s software development where visual studio required one server room and on-call rotations to current continuous build and cloud paradigms.
  • Terminology:
    • engineering bandwidth
    • bottlenecks
    • verification
    • cross-functional (XFN)
  • Why it matters: Understanding where bottlenecks have moved prevents engineering teams from over-optimizing around obsolete constraints like manual test writing order or restrictive code merge queues.

Norms We Had to Rewrite

  • Explanation: Five core systems assuming engineering time was scarce had to change: Code review, onboarding, planning, hiring, and org shape.
  • Key claims:
    • Human judgment on what actually needs code review.
    • Cost of asking a dumb question went to zero during onboarding.
    • Planning requires less upfront design docs and more prototyping.
    • Hiring shifts toward creativity and judgment over raw output.
    • Org shape becomes flatter with every manager acting as an IC first.
  • Examples:
    • Replacing upfront design docs with prototypes and pull requests.
    • Using Claude as a design and content partner during bug fixes.
  • Terminology:
    • planning norms
    • code ownership
    • code review
    • team make-up
    • knowledge sharing
  • Why it matters: Old processes quietly stop working when AI changes throughput velocity; teams must explicitly audit and retire redundant rituals.

How We Rolled It Out

  • Explanation: Rollout combined top-down mandatory principles ('forcing functions') with bottom-up room to adapt for individual pods.
  • Key claims:
    • Every engineer uses Claude Code and Co-work daily.
    • Claudify everything you can.
    • Provide explicit permission to kill old processes.
  • Examples:
    • Mandating that every engineer uses Claude Code while allowing individual teams to adapt their triage, standups, and planning rituals.
  • Terminology:
    • forcing function
    • Claudify
    • team triage
    • bottom-up adaptation
  • Why it matters: Balancing top-down alignment with bottom-up flexibility ensures adoption without suffocating team autonomy.

The Proof: Metrics to Baseline

  • Explanation: Adoption success can be measured by monitoring onboarding ramp time, PR cycle time, and Claude-assisted commit volume.
  • Key claims:
    • Onboarding ramp time goes down because engineers ship real code in week one.
    • PR cycle time shortens and queue depth stops being a leading complaint.
    • Claude-assisted commits become the default rather than the exception.
  • Examples:
    • Tracking whether new engineers land PRs materially faster than a year ago.
  • Terminology:
    • onboarding ramp time
    • PR cycle time
    • Claude-assisted commits
    • shift left
  • Why it matters: Without measurable indicators like ramp time and commit volume, leadership cannot verify if AI-native adoption is truly working.

Audit Your Own Efforts

  • Explanation: Leaders should continuously audit their organization's workflows, question legacy SLAs, dogfood their own products, and keep teams as flat as possible.
  • Key claims:
    • Pick your noisiest workflow and ask if it still earns its place.
    • If Claude can do it, Claude should do it to free humans up for harder work.
    • People don't delete processes on their own; leaders must name the ones that can go.
  • Examples:
    • Auditing multiple incident response and bug fix SLAs to see if they are still necessary in an AI-native workflow.
  • Terminology:
    • dogfooding
    • noisist workflow
    • SLAs
    • shift left
  • Why it matters: Process bloat accumulates naturally over time, and proactive auditing prevents teams from drowning in obsolete bureaucracy.

Key Points

In technical debates, code wins

  • Explanation: When teammates disagree on a design, having Claude prototype both approaches and examining the actual artifact is faster and cheaper than lengthy arguments.
  • Evidence: Generating multiple PR versions with Claude to compare technical approaches and human impact.
  • Practical implication: Reduces meeting time and opinion-driven stalemates by leaning on rapid prototyping.

Code is the new source of truth

  • Explanation: Documentation and design docs quickly go out of date, whereas keeping specs and source of truth directly inside the codebase leverages AI updating loops.
  • Evidence: Claude code commits and repository-embedded specs act as the primary knowledge base for onboarding.
  • Practical implication: Eliminates out-of-sync wikis and ensures engineering documentation stays current.

Every manager starts as an IC

  • Explanation: Managers must stay hands-on with coding and dogfooding to coach scrappiness effectively and understand team velocity.
  • Evidence: Managers on the Claude Code team actively write code, review PRs, and use the tooling daily.
  • Practical implication: Builds authentic product sense and empathy for developer friction points.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Forcing Function Rollout Framework

  • How it works: Combines non-negotiable top-down mandates with bottom-up operational autonomy.
  • Components:
    • Every engineer uses Claude Code
    • Claudify everything you can
    • Explicit permission to kill old processes
    • Room for teams to adapt rituals
  • When to use: When introducing transformative AI tooling across an engineering organization to drive adoption while respecting team nuance.

Examples & Case Studies

Fiona attempted to update CLI tooling with a holiday theme and wanted to make Claude look like a snowman, but a designer reviewed it and pointed out it looked like Mr. Peanut.

  • Illustrates: The necessity of human taste and product sense even when AI handles execution.
  • Lesson: Humans are still essential for taste, brand alignment, risk tolerance, and legal review.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Pick your noisiest workflow on Monday and question if it still earns its place.
    • Dogfood your own product relentlessly to build product sense.
    • Replace upfront design docs with rapid prototypes and PR discussions.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift verification left and automate quality checks closer to the source.
    • Maintain flat organizational structures where managers remain active ICs.
    • Treat code as the primary source of truth for knowledge sharing.
  • Questions to investigate:

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Onboarding ramp time is materially faster than a year ago with new engineers shipping real code in week one. (empirical observation)
  • Queue depth in PR cycle time stopped being a leading complaint after adopting AI-assisted workflows. (empirical observation)

Notable Quotes

"What served you prior, may no longer." "In technical debates, code wins." "If Claude can do it, Claude should. That frees us up for the harder work." "People don't delete processes on their own. They pile new ones on top. Name the ones that can go."

Compressed Summary

  • Engineering bottlenecks shifted from writing code to verification, review, and cross-functional alignment.
  • Five team norms rewritten: code review, onboarding, planning, hiring, and org shape.
  • Building is cheap and arguing is expensive; let code win technical debates.
  • Code is the new source of truth for onboarding and documentation.
  • Leaders must dogfood products, keep teams flat, and aggressively prune obsolete processes.
  • Keywords: ai-native, engineering, claude, workflow, verification
  • Core insight: When AI tooling removes coding bottlenecks, engineering organizations must fundamentally rewrite their planning, review, onboarding, and organizational norms around verification and rapid prototyping.

## Topic Map
### The Shift in Bottlenecks
- **Explanation**: Engineering bandwidth used to be the expensive limiting factor, driving heavy planning, scoping, and review processes to protect that resource. With AI coding tools like Claude Code, coding is rarely the slow part anymore, causing bottlenecks to shift from writing code to verification, review, cross-functional alignment, and security.
- **Key claims**:
  - For years, engineering bandwidth was the expensive thing.
  - On the Claude Code team, coding is rarely the slow part anymore.
  - The bottleneck moved from coding to everything around coding: Verification, Review, XFN, Security.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing early 2000s software development where visual studio required one server room and on-call rotations to current continuous build and cloud paradigms.
- **Terminology**:
  - engineering bandwidth
  - bottlenecks
  - verification
  - cross-functional (XFN)
- **Why it matters**: Understanding where bottlenecks have moved prevents engineering teams from over-optimizing around obsolete constraints like manual test writing order or restrictive code merge queues.
### Norms We Had to Rewrite
- **Explanation**: Five core systems assuming engineering time was scarce had to change: Code review, onboarding, planning, hiring, and org shape.
- **Key claims**:
  - Human judgment on what actually needs code review.
  - Cost of asking a dumb question went to zero during onboarding.
  - Planning requires less upfront design docs and more prototyping.
  - Hiring shifts toward creativity and judgment over raw output.
  - Org shape becomes flatter with every manager acting as an IC first.
- **Examples**:
  - Replacing upfront design docs with prototypes and pull requests.
  - Using Claude as a design and content partner during bug fixes.
- **Terminology**:
  - planning norms
  - code ownership
  - code review
  - team make-up
  - knowledge sharing
- **Why it matters**: Old processes quietly stop working when AI changes throughput velocity; teams must explicitly audit and retire redundant rituals.
### How We Rolled It Out
- **Explanation**: Rollout combined top-down mandatory principles ('forcing functions') with bottom-up room to adapt for individual pods.
- **Key claims**:
  - Every engineer uses Claude Code and Co-work daily.
  - Claudify everything you can.
  - Provide explicit permission to kill old processes.
- **Examples**:
  - Mandating that every engineer uses Claude Code while allowing individual teams to adapt their triage, standups, and planning rituals.
- **Terminology**:
  - forcing function
  - Claudify
  - team triage
  - bottom-up adaptation
- **Why it matters**: Balancing top-down alignment with bottom-up flexibility ensures adoption without suffocating team autonomy.
### The Proof: Metrics to Baseline
- **Explanation**: Adoption success can be measured by monitoring onboarding ramp time, PR cycle time, and Claude-assisted commit volume.
- **Key claims**:
  - Onboarding ramp time goes down because engineers ship real code in week one.
  - PR cycle time shortens and queue depth stops being a leading complaint.
  - Claude-assisted commits become the default rather than the exception.
- **Examples**:
  - Tracking whether new engineers land PRs materially faster than a year ago.
- **Terminology**:
  - onboarding ramp time
  - PR cycle time
  - Claude-assisted commits
  - shift left
- **Why it matters**: Without measurable indicators like ramp time and commit volume, leadership cannot verify if AI-native adoption is truly working.
### Audit Your Own Efforts
- **Explanation**: Leaders should continuously audit their organization's workflows, question legacy SLAs, dogfood their own products, and keep teams as flat as possible.
- **Key claims**:
  - Pick your noisiest workflow and ask if it still earns its place.
  - If Claude can do it, Claude should do it to free humans up for harder work.
  - People don't delete processes on their own; leaders must name the ones that can go.
- **Examples**:
  - Auditing multiple incident response and bug fix SLAs to see if they are still necessary in an AI-native workflow.
- **Terminology**:
  - dogfooding
  - noisist workflow
  - SLAs
  - shift left
- **Why it matters**: Process bloat accumulates naturally over time, and proactive auditing prevents teams from drowning in obsolete bureaucracy.
## Key Points
### In technical debates, code wins
- **Explanation**: When teammates disagree on a design, having Claude prototype both approaches and examining the actual artifact is faster and cheaper than lengthy arguments.
- **Evidence**: Generating multiple PR versions with Claude to compare technical approaches and human impact.
- **Practical implication**: Reduces meeting time and opinion-driven stalemates by leaning on rapid prototyping.
### Code is the new source of truth
- **Explanation**: Documentation and design docs quickly go out of date, whereas keeping specs and source of truth directly inside the codebase leverages AI updating loops.
- **Evidence**: Claude code commits and repository-embedded specs act as the primary knowledge base for onboarding.
- **Practical implication**: Eliminates out-of-sync wikis and ensures engineering documentation stays current.
### Every manager starts as an IC
- **Explanation**: Managers must stay hands-on with coding and dogfooding to coach scrappiness effectively and understand team velocity.
- **Evidence**: Managers on the Claude Code team actively write code, review PRs, and use the tooling daily.
- **Practical implication**: Builds authentic product sense and empathy for developer friction points.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Forcing Function Rollout Framework
- **How it works**: Combines non-negotiable top-down mandates with bottom-up operational autonomy.
- **Components**:
  - Every engineer uses Claude Code
  - Claudify everything you can
  - Explicit permission to kill old processes
  - Room for teams to adapt rituals
- **When to use**: When introducing transformative AI tooling across an engineering organization to drive adoption while respecting team nuance.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Fiona attempted to update CLI tooling with a holiday theme and wanted to make Claude look like a snowman, but a designer reviewed it and pointed out it looked like Mr. Peanut.
- **Illustrates**: The necessity of human taste and product sense even when AI handles execution.
- **Lesson**: Humans are still essential for taste, brand alignment, risk tolerance, and legal review.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Pick your noisiest workflow on Monday and question if it still earns its place.
  - Dogfood your own product relentlessly to build product sense.
  - Replace upfront design docs with rapid prototypes and PR discussions.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift verification left and automate quality checks closer to the source.
  - Maintain flat organizational structures where managers remain active ICs.
  - Treat code as the primary source of truth for knowledge sharing.

## Compressed Summary
- Engineering bottlenecks shifted from writing code to verification, review, and cross-functional alignment.
- Five team norms rewritten: code review, onboarding, planning, hiring, and org shape.
- Building is cheap and arguing is expensive; let code win technical debates.
- Code is the new source of truth for onboarding and documentation.
- Leaders must dogfood products, keep teams flat, and aggressively prune obsolete processes.
- **Keywords**: ai-native, engineering, claude, workflow, verification
- **Core insight**: When AI tooling removes coding bottlenecks, engineering organizations must fundamentally rewrite their planning, review, onboarding, and organizational norms around verification and rapid prototyping.
